sections.title: Definition and the factor VIII–VWF partnership

blocks.text: **Haemophilia A** is an inherited lack of coagulation **factor VIII**. **Haemophilia B** (Christmas disease) is the same disorder caused by too little **factor IX**, and the two cannot be told apart clinically. Together they are the **commonest congenital deficiencies of a single coagulation factor**. The commonest inherited bleeding disorder overall is still **von Willebrand disease (VWD)**.

blocks.title: Factor VIII and IX essentials
items: Factor VIII is produced mainly by the **liver and endothelial cells**
Plasma half-life is about **12 hours** for factor VIII and about **18 hours** for factor IX
In plasma, factor VIII travels **bound to von Willebrand factor (VWF)**, which shields it from proteolysis
In haemophilia A, **VWF is normal** and only the factor VIII coagulant activity (VIII:C) is low. Normal factor VIII is about **50–150 IU/dL**

blocks.title: The haemophilias at a glance
rows: Clinically identical to A but rarer; X-linked recessive
Most frequent in Ashkenazi Jewish people; often autosomal recessive
Not inherited; linked to autoimmune disease, lymphoproliferative disorders, cancer or the postpartum period

blocks.note: Look at: VIII:C and VWF made separately. In haemophilia A, VIII:C is defective but VWF is normal. In VWD, low VWF leaves factor VIII unprotected, so it is cleared quickly.

blocks.text: A **single** low factor suggests an **inherited** disorder. **Several** low factors suggest an **acquired** cause such as liver failure, vitamin K deficiency or DIC.

blocks.title: How common is haemophilia?
rows: Rarer than A (A is about 80% of cases)

blocks.text: The books give different incidence figures. **Davidson's quotes 1 in 10 000** for haemophilia A, while Kumar & Clark and K&C Essentials say 1 in 5000 males. Quote Davidson's in the exam, and remember that **B is several times rarer than A**.

The genes for factor VIII and factor IX are both on the **X chromosome**, so both haemophilias are **X-linked recessive**. Affected patients are almost always **male**, and women are usually carriers.

blocks.title: Pedigree rules
items: **Carrier mother:** each son has a **50%** chance of being affected and each daughter a **50%** chance of being a carrier
Put another way, each pregnancy of a carrier carries a **1 in 4** chance each of an affected boy, an unaffected boy, a carrier girl or a non-carrier girl
**Affected father:** every daughter is an **obligate carrier** and every son is unaffected (the father passes his Y chromosome to his sons)
Haemophilia **breeds true**: everyone in a family shares the same mutation and has a similar severity

blocks.title: Genetics and carrier testing
items: An **intron 22 inversion** of the factor VIII gene accounts for about **half of families with severe haemophilia A**. Other lesions include deletions and missense, nonsense and splice-site mutations
The mutation rate is high: about **one-third of cases have no family history**
Carriers may have a **low factor VIII** from random X-inactivation (lyonization) and a mild bleeding tendency, so **measure factor VIII in every known or suspected carrier**
Because carrier factor VIII levels overlap with normal, **definitive carrier status comes from mutation analysis**
**Antenatal diagnosis:** chorionic villus sampling at 11–12 weeks when the family mutation is known and termination would be considered; otherwise amniocentesis in the third trimester

blocks.text: **A negative family history does not exclude haemophilia.** About one-third of cases arise from a new mutation.
Contrast with VWD: its gene is on **chromosome 12** and inheritance is mostly **autosomal dominant**. Types 2N and 3 are autosomal recessive.

blocks.note: Look at: Queen Victoria's pedigree. Haemophilia B passes through carrier daughters to affected grandsons (X-linked recessive pattern).

blocks.title: Severity grading (ISTH, Davidson Box 23.63)
rows: Spontaneous haemarthroses and muscle haematomas from early childhood
Bleeding after minor trauma or surgery; occasional spontaneous bleeds
Excess bleeding only after major injury or surgery; often diagnosed late

blocks.title: Pattern of bleeding
items: Classic presentation: a **boy who has just started walking (1–2 years)** with spontaneous bleeding into joints and muscles
**Haemarthrosis** of large joints: **knee (commonest)**, elbow, ankle and hip
**Muscle haematomas**, typically in the **calf and psoas**
An untreated bleed gives a **hot, swollen, very painful** joint or muscle
**Retroperitoneal** and **intracranial** haemorrhage, plus haematuria and GI bleeding
Bleeding in mild and moderate disease follows the same pattern but needs trauma or surgery, and it is out of proportion to the injury

blocks.text: **Site and timing point to the defect.** Joint, muscle, retroperitoneal or intracranial bleeding suggests a **coagulation factor** defect, while purpura, epistaxis, menorrhagia and mucosal bleeding suggest **platelets or VWD**. Bleeding that starts **after a delay** following surgery suggests a coagulation defect; **immediate** bleeding suggests a platelet plug problem.

**Newborns** with severe haemophilia have a higher risk of intracranial haemorrhage. Routine caesarean section is **not** required, but head trauma should be avoided and the baby's head **imaged within 24 hours** of birth.
**Mild haemophilia** may cause no symptoms until a dental extraction, surgery or trauma in adult life. A normal childhood does not exclude it.

The upper limit for 'mild' differs between books. **Davidson's (ISTH) uses > 0.05–0.4 U/mL (5–40%)**, Pocket Medicine 5–25% and Step-Up 5–10% (with a separate 'subclinical' band at about 10%). All agree that severe is < 1% and moderate 1–5%. Use Davidson's cut-offs.

blocks.note: Look at: chronic arthropathy with swelling and muscle wasting, a thigh muscle haematoma, massive bruising and a retroperitoneal bleed.

blocks.text: The typical result is an **isolated prolonged APTT** (reference about 26–36 s) with a **normal PT** (about 9–12 s), a normal bleeding time and **normal VWF**. A **specific factor assay** shows a low factor VIII (or IX), which confirms the diagnosis and grades its severity.

blocks.title: Why only the APTT is long
items: Factors **VIII, IX and XI** belong to the intrinsic pathway, which the APTT measures
The APTT is also prolonged by deficiency of XII (and of II, V, X), **unfractionated heparin**, antibodies against clotting factors and **lupus anticoagulant**
The PT tests the tissue-factor (extrinsic) pathway, factors II, V, VII and X, and stays **normal** in haemophilia

blocks.title: The mixing study (1:1 with normal plasma)
rows: Factor **deficiency** (normal plasma supplies the missing factor)
Haemophilia A or B, factor XI deficiency. Next: specific factor assays
Heparin, lupus anticoagulant, or a specific anti-factor VIII antibody (acquired haemophilia or an inhibitor in treated haemophilia). The **Bethesda assay** measures its titre

blocks.alt: Algorithm: an isolated prolonged APTT goes to a 1:1 mix with normal plasma. If it corrects, it is a factor deficiency, so assay VIII, IX and XI. If not, an inhibitor is present, quantified with the Bethesda assay.

blocks.text: Exam ladder: after an isolated long APTT, the **best initial test is a mixing study** and the **most accurate test is a specific factor assay** (VIII, IX).

blocks.note: Look at: a flowchart for working up a prolonged aPTT, with a mixing study followed by specific factor assays.

blocks.title: Haemophilia A vs VWD vs vitamin K deficiency
Von Willebrand disease: the main mimic
items: The **commonest inherited bleeding disorder** (about 1% of the population)
Low VWF **secondarily lowers factor VIII**, because VWF carries and protects it
Bleeding is **mucocutaneous** (bruising, epistaxis, menorrhagia, GI, after dental work) and usually milder than in haemophilia
**Haemarthroses are rare**, even in severe type 3 disease
Ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation is reduced; the ristocetin cofactor assay helps separate VWD from platelet disorders
**Type 2N** (VWF cannot bind factor VIII, autosomal recessive) gives a low factor VIII and can **mimic haemophilia A**

blocks.title: Other causes of a coagulopathy (Davidson Box 23.62)
rows: Other inherited factor deficiencies (II, V, VII, X, XI, XIII)
Autosomal; factor XI deficiency (haemophilia C) is commoner in Ashkenazi Jews
Low II, VII, IX, X with V and VIII normal; **PT and APTT both prolonged**; treat with phytomenadione
Consumption of **all** factors, **including V and VIII**
Autoantibody against VIII; APTT does **not** correct on mixing

blocks.text: VWD can present with a **normal APTT**, so a normal coagulation screen does not exclude it.
**Haemophilia A and B look identical at the bedside.** Only a factor assay separates them, and this matters because **desmopressin is useless in haemophilia B**.

blocks.note: Look at: the table of bleeding time, PT, APTT, VIII:C and VWF in haemophilia A, VWD and vitamin K deficiency. A classic OSPE lab-interpretation grid.
Look at: where VWF, platelet and COX/TXA2 defects act, which separates primary (platelet/VWF) defects from factor deficiencies.

blocks.title: Musculoskeletal: the main long-term morbidity
items: Repeated haemarthroses cause **synovial hypertrophy**, **cartilage destruction** and **chronic haemophilic arthropathy**, with deformity, arthritis and crippling disability
X-ray: loss of joint space, sclerosis, osteophytes, bone cysts and widened femoral epicondyles
A large **psoas haematoma** can compress the **femoral nerve**
A **calf haematoma** in its tight fascial sheath can cause **compartment syndrome**, leading to ischaemia, necrosis, fibrosis and a **shortened Achilles tendon**

blocks.title: Life-threatening bleeding
items: **Intracranial haemorrhage** is much commoner than in the general population and is a major cause of death
Treat **any head injury** as potentially life-threatening and assess it urgently
Retroperitoneal haemorrhage can be massive

blocks.title: Inhibitors (alloantibodies to infused factor)
rows: About **20% of severe** cases (Davidson); up to 30% over a lifetime (Kumar), usually after the first few doses; rare in mild or moderate disease
Infused factor VIII stops working; APTT not corrected on mixing
May first appear as a **severe allergic-type reaction** to factor IX
Bypassing agents: **recombinant VIIa** or **FEIBA** (activated prothrombin complex)

blocks.text: Inhibitor rates differ: **Davidson's says about 20% of severe haemophilia A**, Kumar says up to 30% over a lifetime and K&C Essentials 10% of all people with haemophilia. Quote Davidson's 20%, and remember that inhibitors are **rare in haemophilia B**.

blocks.title: Infections transmitted by blood products
items: Concentrates were **not virally inactivated before 1986**
Among those treated with non-inactivated pooled concentrate before 1988: **HCV almost universal**, **80–90% HBV exposure**, **60% HIV-positive**
Long-term result: cirrhosis and **hepatocellular carcinoma** from HCV
Today: donor screening for HBV, HCV and HIV, two viral-inactivation steps and recombinant products. The risk is now almost eliminated
**vCJD** was transmitted to one recipient of factor VIII, so plasma is now sourced from countries with little bovine spongiform encephalopathy

blocks.text: With modern treatment, **life expectancy is very good**. The main causes of death are now **cancer and heart disease**, although cerebral haemorrhage is still more frequent than in the general population.

blocks.note: Look at: knee X-ray of advanced haemophilic arthropathy (no cartilage space, sclerosis, osteophytes, cysts, widened epicondyles) and a hepatoma in an HCV-cirrhotic liver.

blocks.title: General principles
items: Register the patient at a **comprehensive haemophilia care centre**
For pain, use analgesia that **avoids aspirin and NSAIDs**
Vaccinate non-immune recipients of pooled products against **hepatitis A and B**
Encourage exercise but **avoid contact sports**

blocks.title: Factor replacement strategies
rows: **Prophylaxis** (standard of care in severe A or B where affordable)

Keep the **trough factor level > 0.02 U/mL**. Start in early childhood (around 2 years) with home IV factor VIII at least 3 times a week, or factor IX twice a week. This cuts bleeds and slows joint damage

Treat each bleed by raising the factor level with IV concentrate. Freeze-dried concentrate is stable at 4°C, so patients keep it at home and treat at the first sign of bleeding. Still used where resources are limited
Keep factor VIII in the normal range until healing; because the half-life is ~12 h it is often given **twice daily**

**Recombinant** concentrates are preferred to plasma-derived ones. Extended half-life products (Fc fusion, pegylation; albumin fusion for IX) last ~1.5× longer for VIII and 3–5× longer for IX, which allows weekly or two-weekly IX dosing

blocks.title: Acute haemarthrosis
items: Give **factor concentrate as soon as possible**
**Rest** the joint with bed rest or a splint, and apply ice
Use analgesia that **avoids aspirin and NSAIDs**
Once bleeding settles, mobilise with **physiotherapy** to rebuild muscle strength
Surgical decompression may be needed for a severe bleed

blocks.title: Desmopressin (DDAVP) in haemophilia A
rows: Releases stored VWF and factor VIII, raising them **3–4-fold** (Kumar: 3–5-fold)
**Mild or moderate haemophilia A**; works best when baseline factor VIII is > 10 IU/dL
**0.3 μg/kg IV or SC**, or **300 μg intranasally** (higher than the dose for diabetes insipidus)
**Water retention and hyponatraemia** after repeated doses
**Severe arterial disease** (thrombosis risk) and **young children** (hyponatraemic seizures)

blocks.text: Davidson's and First Aid allow desmopressin in **mild or moderate** haemophilia A. K&C Essentials, Step-Up and Pocket Medicine mention only mild disease. Follow Davidson's, and **never use it for haemophilia B**.

blocks.title: Inhibitors and newer therapies
items: Bleeds with an inhibitor: **bypassing agents**, either **recombinant factor VIIa** or **activated prothrombin complex concentrate (FEIBA)**. Porcine factor VIII is another option for high titres
Low-titre inhibitors may be overcome with **high doses of factor**, with plasmapheresis or immunosuppression as further options
**Immune tolerance induction** eradicates the inhibitor in about 80%
**Emicizumab**, a bispecific antibody that bridges factors IX and X and so does factor VIII's job, gives prophylaxis in haemophilia A **with or without inhibitors**
**Gene therapy** with an adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector carrying a factor VIII or high-activity factor IX gene is promising

blocks.title: Adjuncts and second-line products
items: **Antifibrinolytics** (tranexamic acid, aminocaproic acid) are adjuncts, especially for mucosal bleeding
**Cryoprecipitate** (factor VIII 80–120 U per pack, plus fibrinogen) or **FFP** only when virus-inactivated or recombinant concentrate is unavailable
Haemophilia B: **factor IX concentrate**, used the same way as factor VIII (cryoprecipitate's listed contents, mainly fibrinogen, factor VIII and VWF with some factor XIII, do not include factor IX)

blocks.text: Match the product to the factor: **VIII for A, IX for B**. **Desmopressin helps only A**, and an inhibitor calls for a **bypassing agent** (rVIIa or FEIBA).

cards.front: Which factor is deficient in haemophilia A, and which in haemophilia B?
cards.back: A: **factor VIII**. B (Christmas disease): **factor IX**

cards.front: Approximate plasma half-life of factor VIII, and of factor IX?
cards.back: VIII: about **12 h**. IX: about **18 h**

cards.front: Why does von Willebrand disease lower factor VIII?
cards.back: VWF **carries factor VIII and protects it** from proteolysis, so with low VWF factor VIII is cleared quickly

cards.front: Incidence of haemophilia A (Davidson's)?
cards.back: About **1 in 10 000**. Haemophilia B is rarer (about 1 in 30 000 males)

cards.front: Children of a man with haemophilia and a non-carrier woman?
cards.back: All **daughters are obligate carriers**; all **sons are unaffected**

cards.front: Outcome per pregnancy for a carrier woman and an unaffected man?
cards.back: **1 in 4** each: affected boy, unaffected boy, carrier girl, non-carrier girl

cards.front: What proportion of haemophilia has no family history?
cards.back: About **one-third** (high new-mutation rate)

cards.front: Commonest mutation in severe haemophilia A?
cards.back: **Intron 22 inversion** of the factor VIII gene (about 50% of severe families)

cards.front: ISTH severity cut-offs for factor VIII/IX?
Commonest sites of joint and muscle bleeds in haemophilia?
cards.back: Joints: **knee**, elbow, ankle, hip. Muscles: **calf and psoas**

cards.front: What does delayed (not immediate) post-operative bleeding suggest?
cards.back: A **coagulation factor defect** (immediate bleeding suggests a platelet plug defect)

cards.front: Classic coagulation results in haemophilia A?
cards.back: **Isolated prolonged APTT**, low factor VIII; PT, bleeding time and VWF **normal**

cards.front: A prolonged APTT corrects on 1:1 mixing with normal plasma. What does that mean?
cards.back: A **factor deficiency**. Failure to correct means an **inhibitor** (heparin, lupus anticoagulant, anti-VIII)

cards.front: Which two tests separate VWD from haemophilia A?
cards.back: **Bleeding time** (prolonged in VWD) and **VWF level** (low in VWD); both are normal in haemophilia

cards.front: Which VWD subtype mimics haemophilia A, and why?
cards.back: **Type 2N**: VWF cannot bind factor VIII, so factor VIII is low (autosomal recessive)

cards.front: Which factor stays normal in liver failure but falls in DIC?
cards.back: **Factor VIII**

cards.front: Inhibitor frequency in severe haemophilia A (Davidson's) vs haemophilia B?
cards.back: A: about **20%**. B: **< 1%**, sometimes heralded by an allergic-type reaction

cards.front: Nerve compressed by a large psoas haematoma?
cards.back: The **femoral nerve**

cards.front: Target trough level for prophylaxis in severe haemophilia?
cards.back: Factor VIII (or IX) **above 0.02 U/mL**

cards.front: Haemostatic dose of desmopressin, and two contraindications?
cards.back: **0.3 μg/kg IV/SC** or **300 μg intranasally**. Contraindicated in **severe arterial disease** and **young children**

cards.front: How does emicizumab work?
cards.back: A **bispecific antibody bridging factors IX and X**, mimicking factor VIII; prophylaxis in haemophilia A with or without inhibitors

cards.front: Treatment of a bleed in a patient with a factor VIII inhibitor?
cards.back: A **bypassing agent**: recombinant factor VIIa or FEIBA (aPCC)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has had two episodes of a hot, swollen knee after minor falls. APTT is prolonged and PT is normal. Factor VIII activity is normal, but another intrinsic-pathway factor is below 1% of normal.
questions.leadIn: Which coagulation factor is most likely deficient?
questions.explanation: A boy with spontaneous haemarthroses, an isolated long APTT and normal factor VIII has **haemophilia B (factor IX deficiency)**. It is clinically identical to haemophilia A.
whyNot: Factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT, not the APTT alone.
Factor XII deficiency prolongs the APTT, but it is not one of the haemophilias; spontaneous joint bleeds in a boy point to the X-linked factors VIII and IX.
Low VWF would also lower factor VIII and gives mucocutaneous bleeding, not joint bleeds.
Severe fibrinogen deficiency prolongs both PT and APTT.

questions.stem: A student is revising why patients with von Willebrand disease often have low factor VIII levels.
questions.leadIn: Which statement about factor VIII is correct?
options: It is made mainly by the liver and endothelial cells
Its plasma half-life is about 72 hours
Its synthesis depends on vitamin K
It is produced only by megakaryocytes
questions.explanation: Factor VIII comes mainly from the **liver and endothelium**, has a half-life of about **12 h**, and is protected in plasma by binding to **VWF**. That is why VWD lowers it.
whyNot: The half-life is about 12 hours, which is why surgical dosing is twice daily.
Its carrier protein is von Willebrand factor, not fibrinogen.
Vitamin K-dependent factors are II, VII, IX and X; factor VIII is normal in vitamin K deficiency.
Megakaryocytes (with endothelium) make VWF, not factor VIII.

questions.stem: A man with severe haemophilia A and his wife, who has no family history of bleeding and a normal factor VIII level, are expecting a daughter.
questions.leadIn: What is the probability that their daughter is a carrier of haemophilia A?
questions.explanation: An affected father passes his only X chromosome, which carries the mutant factor VIII gene, to **every daughter**. All his daughters are therefore **obligate carriers**.
whyNot: She must inherit her father's X chromosome, so she cannot escape carrying the mutation.
One in four is the chance of an affected boy per pregnancy for a carrier mother, not this situation.
Fifty per cent applies to daughters of a carrier mother, not of an affected father.
There is no pedigree in which 75% applies here.

questions.stem: A 7-month-old boy has a large forearm haematoma after a vaccination. Factor VIII activity is below 1%. Neither parent nor any relative has ever had a bleeding problem.
questions.leadIn: Which statement best explains the absent family history?
options: About one-third of haemophilia cases arise from a new mutation
Haemophilia A is autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance
Severe haemophilia skips generations because of genomic imprinting
The father must be a silent carrier
Absent family history makes haemophilia A unlikely, so the result is probably wrong
questions.explanation: Because the factor VIII gene has a **high mutation rate**, about **one-third of cases are sporadic**. A negative family history never excludes haemophilia.
whyNot: Haemophilia A is X-linked recessive.
Imprinting plays no part. The disease passes silently through carrier females, but here there is no history at all.
Fathers cannot pass an X-linked disorder to their sons, and males with the mutation are affected rather than silent carriers.
A factor VIII level below 1% is diagnostic; a negative family history does not exclude the disease.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man had prolonged bleeding needing re-suturing after removal of his wisdom teeth. He has never bled spontaneously. APTT is mildly prolonged and factor VIII is 0.15 U/mL.
questions.leadIn: How should his haemophilia A be graded?
options: Cannot be graded without a factor IX level
questions.explanation: Factor VIII **> 0.05–0.4 U/mL** is **mild** haemophilia (ISTH). Excess bleeding only after surgery or trauma, first noticed in adulthood, fits this grade.
whyNot: Severe means < 0.01 U/mL with spontaneous joint and muscle bleeds.
Moderate means 0.01–0.05 U/mL.
0.15 U/mL is below normal and lies within the mild range.
Grading uses the deficient factor alone; factor IX is irrelevant in haemophilia A.

questions.stem: A doctor is taking a bleeding history from a patient referred with easy bleeding.
questions.leadIn: Which feature most strongly suggests a coagulation factor deficiency rather than a platelet or VWF disorder?
options: Spontaneous swelling of the knee joint
Immediate prolonged oozing from a small cut
questions.explanation: Bleeding into **joints and muscles** (and retroperitoneal or intracranial bleeding) points to a **coagulation factor** defect. Mucocutaneous bleeding and immediate oozing point to primary haemostasis.
whyNot: Petechiae suggest thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction.
Mucosal bleeding suggests a platelet or VWF defect.
Menorrhagia is a classic mucocutaneous symptom of VWD or platelet disorders.
Immediate bleeding suggests a failure of platelet plug formation; coagulation defects tend to bleed after a delay.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy has a swollen ankle after a minor knock. APTT is 72 s (reference 26–36 s), PT is 11 s, platelet count is normal and the film is unremarkable.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: An **isolated prolonged APTT** is followed first by a **mixing study**. Correction points to a factor deficiency and directs the specific factor assays.
whyNot: The film and platelet count are normal, so a marrow examination adds nothing.
Platelet function tests do not explain a prolonged APTT.
A D-dimer looks for DIC, which would also prolong the PT and lower platelets.
The INR is only for monitoring coumarin therapy and is not a screening test.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with a swollen ankle after a minor knock has an isolated prolonged APTT that corrects completely after a 1:1 mix with normal plasma.
questions.leadIn: Which test will confirm the diagnosis most accurately?
options: Specific factor VIII and IX assays
questions.explanation: Correction on mixing indicates a **factor deficiency**. The **specific factor assay** is the most accurate test: it identifies the factor and grades severity.
whyNot: A Bethesda assay measures an inhibitor, but correction on mixing shows no inhibitor is present.
The thrombin time assesses fibrinogen conversion and is normal in haemophilia.
Fibrinogen is normal in haemophilia; the PT would be long if it were very low.
Bleeding time tests platelet function and is normal in haemophilia.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman has had heavy periods since menarche, frequent nosebleeds and prolonged bleeding after a dental extraction. Her mother has similar symptoms. Bleeding time is prolonged, APTT is mildly prolonged, PT is normal, and factor VIII:C and VWF antigen are both reduced.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Mucocutaneous bleeding, **autosomal dominant** inheritance (mother affected), a **prolonged bleeding time** and **low VWF with secondarily low VIII** are the hallmarks of **VWD**.
whyNot: A carrier may have a low factor VIII, but VWF and bleeding time would be normal.
ITP gives thrombocytopenia with a normal APTT and VWF.
Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT and leaves VIII and VWF normal.
Haemophilia B affects factor IX, with normal VWF and bleeding time.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman with no previous bleeding history develops extensive spontaneous bruising and a large forearm haematoma. APTT is prolonged and stays prolonged after a 1:1 mix with normal plasma. PT and platelet count are normal; factor VIII is very low.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: New bleeding late in life with a low factor VIII and an APTT that **does not correct on mixing** indicates an **autoantibody against factor VIII**, which is acquired haemophilia A.
whyNot: Inherited haemophilia would cause lifelong bleeding, and its APTT corrects on mixing.
VWD causes mucocutaneous bleeding from youth, and the APTT corrects on mixing.
Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT with normal factor VIII.
DIC lowers platelets and prolongs the PT as well as the APTT.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with severe haemophilia A falls during football. He develops groin pain, keeps his hip flexed, and has numbness over the front of the thigh with weak knee extension.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of the neurological signs?
options: Iliopsoas haematoma compressing the femoral nerve
questions.explanation: A large **psoas bleed** can extend to compress the **femoral nerve**, causing anterior thigh numbness and quadriceps weakness.
whyNot: A haemarthrosis gives a hot swollen joint but no femoral nerve deficit.
A calf haematoma affects the lower leg and Achilles tendon, not the thigh.
The sciatic nerve supplies the posterior thigh and below the knee, not knee extension.
A spinal haematoma would give bilateral signs or a sensory level.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with severe haemophilia A on factor VIII prophylaxis has bleeds that no longer respond to his usual doses. The APTT does not correct on mixing with normal plasma. He now has a painful, swollen elbow.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate treatment for this bleed?
questions.explanation: He has developed an **anti-factor VIII inhibitor** (about 20% of severe haemophilia A). Bleeds need a **bypassing agent** such as **recombinant VIIa** or FEIBA.
whyNot: Desmopressin cannot help severe haemophilia A, and the inhibitor would neutralise any factor VIII it released.
The factor VIII in FFP would also be neutralised by the inhibitor.
Factor IX does not bypass a factor VIII inhibitor; activated products are needed.
Platelets are normal; the defect is coagulation.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with mild haemophilia A (factor VIII 0.2 U/mL) needs a dental extraction. He has no cardiovascular disease.
questions.leadIn: Which agent would best raise his factor VIII level for the procedure?
questions.explanation: In **mild or moderate haemophilia A**, desmopressin releases stored VWF and factor VIII, raising them **3–4-fold**. This avoids exposure to factor concentrate.
whyNot: Factor IX is the treatment for haemophilia B.
His vitamin K-dependent factors are normal.
Platelets do not correct a factor VIII deficiency.
Bypassing agents are kept for patients with inhibitors.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with mild haemophilia B (factor IX 0.12 U/mL) is scheduled for elective inguinal hernia repair.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate haemostatic cover?
questions.explanation: Haemophilia B is treated with **factor IX concentrate** (recombinant factor IX is widely available), used in the same way as factor VIII in haemophilia A. Desmopressin does not work in haemophilia B.
whyNot: Desmopressin releases VWF and factor VIII, not factor IX, so it is ineffective in haemophilia B.
Cryoprecipitate supplies mainly fibrinogen, factor VIII and VWF (with some factor XIII), not factor IX.
Factor VIII is not deficient.
An antifibrinolytic does not replace the missing factor IX, so it is not adequate cover on its own.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with severe haemophilia A (factor VIII < 0.01 U/mL) and no inhibitor has had three knee bleeds since he started walking, each treated with factor VIII on demand. His parents ask how to protect his joints in the long term.
questions.leadIn: What is the best long-term strategy?
options: Continue factor VIII only when bleeds occur
Regular prophylactic recombinant factor VIII at least three times a week
questions.explanation: Step 1: grade the disease. A factor VIII level < 0.01 U/mL is **severe**, with spontaneous haemarthroses. Step 2: identify the main long-term harm. Recurrent joint bleeds cause **synovial hypertrophy, cartilage loss and chronic arthropathy**. Step 3: choose the strategy that prevents bleeds. **Prophylaxis** keeps the trough factor VIII **above 0.02 U/mL**, which sharply cuts bleeding episodes and slows joint damage. It starts in early childhood with home infusions at least three times a week, and **recombinant** concentrate is preferred. On-demand treatment is the fallback where prophylaxis is not affordable.
whyNot: On-demand treatment stops each bleed, but joint damage still builds up; it is the fallback where resources are limited.
Desmopressin does nothing in severe disease and is contraindicated in young children because of hyponatraemic seizures.
Antifibrinolytics are only an adjunct and cannot replace factor VIII.
FFP should be used only when concentrate is unavailable, and monthly dosing would not maintain a trough level.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with severe haemophilia A was treated in the early 1980s with pooled plasma-derived factor VIII that had not been virally inactivated. He now has cirrhosis and a liver mass on ultrasound.
questions.leadIn: Which infection is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Among patients treated with non-inactivated pooled concentrates before 1988, **hepatitis C infection was almost universal**. Chronic HCV leads to **cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma**, as in Davidson Fig. 23.32.
whyNot: Hepatitis A immunisation is now offered to recipients of pooled products, but the infection the old concentrates transmitted almost universally was hepatitis C.
About 60% became HIV-positive, but HIV does not itself cause cirrhosis and a liver mass.
vCJD has been transmitted only once by factor VIII and causes a neurological illness.
CMV is not among the infections linked to non-inactivated concentrates (HCV, HBV and HIV).

questions.stem: A woman known to carry severe haemophilia A has an uncomplicated vaginal delivery of a boy. Cord blood later confirms severe haemophilia A.
questions.leadIn: Which step is recommended for the newborn?
options: Cranial imaging within the first 24 hours of life
Routine prophylactic fresh frozen plasma at birth
Immediate elective circumcision to test haemostasis
Factor VIII inhibitor screen on cord blood
Delay any imaging until neurological signs appear
questions.explanation: Babies with severe haemophilia have a higher risk of **intracranial haemorrhage**. Head trauma should be avoided and the **head imaged within 24 hours**. Routine caesarean section is not required.
whyNot: Prophylactic FFP is not recommended; when replacement is needed, recombinant concentrate is preferred.
Circumcision is a major haemostatic challenge and would be dangerous.
Inhibitors develop only after exposure to factor VIII concentrate, usually within the first few doses, so testing at birth is pointless.
Waiting for signs risks missing an intracranial bleed.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has spontaneous bruising. PT and APTT are both prolonged. The team wants to tell liver disease apart from DIC.
questions.leadIn: Which factor would typically be normal in liver disease but low in DIC?
questions.explanation: **Factor VIII** is made partly by endothelium, so it stays **normal in liver failure**. In **DIC** it is **consumed** with all the other factors.
whyNot: Factor VII falls in both liver failure and DIC.
Prothrombin falls in both conditions.
Factor X falls in both conditions.
Factor IX is liver-derived and falls in liver failure as well as DIC.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman, whose brother has severe haemophilia A, bleeds heavily after a tooth extraction. Her father is unaffected. Her factor VIII is 0.3 U/mL and VWF is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation for her low factor VIII?
options: Random inactivation of her normal X chromosome in a carrier
Inheritance of two mutant X chromosomes
Autosomal dominant transmission of the factor VIII mutation
An acquired autoantibody against factor VIII
Blood group O lowering factor VIII directly
questions.explanation: She is probably a **carrier** like her mother. Random X-inactivation (**lyonization**) can silence mostly the normal X, giving a **low factor VIII** and mild bleeding. This is why all suspected carriers have their factor VIII measured.
whyNot: Two mutant X chromosomes would need an affected father, and hers is unaffected.
Haemophilia A is X-linked recessive.
An acquired inhibitor is unlikely given the family history; testing for one would need a mixing study.
Blood group O lowers VWF, but her VWF is normal.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best match from the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 7-year-old boy has recurrent ankle bleeds after minor knocks. Platelet count and bleeding time are normal, PT is normal and APTT is prolonged. The APTT corrects on mixing. Factor VIII is normal and factor IX is 3%.
items.explanation: Step 1: an isolated long APTT localises the problem to the intrinsic pathway (VIII, IX, XI). Step 2: correction on mixing means a deficiency, not an inhibitor. Step 3: the factor assay shows low IX and normal VIII. This is **haemophilia B**, moderate grade (1–5%).

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has had nosebleeds and heavy periods since menarche. Bleeding time is prolonged, APTT is slightly long, PT is normal, and both factor VIII:C and VWF are reduced.
items.explanation: Step 1: mucocutaneous bleeding with a long bleeding time indicates a primary haemostasis problem. Step 2: low VWF explains the low VIII, because VWF carries and protects it. This is **von Willebrand disease**, whereas haemophilia leaves VWF and bleeding time normal.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man in intensive care with sepsis after bowel surgery oozes from cannula sites. Platelets are 40 × 10⁹/L, PT and APTT are both prolonged, fibrinogen is low, and factors V and VIII are both reduced.
items.explanation: Step 1: several factors are low together with thrombocytopenia, which suggests an acquired consumptive process. Step 2: factor VIII is low, so this is not liver failure (VIII is preserved there). Low fibrinogen in a septic patient means **DIC**.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best match from the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 14-month-old boy who has just started walking has a hot, tense left knee after a minor fall and several large bruises. His maternal uncle was "a bleeder". APTT is prolonged and factor VIII is below 1%.
items.explanation: A toddler with a spontaneous haemarthrosis, an X-linked family history through the mother and factor VIII < 1% has **severe haemophilia A**.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man has never had a bleeding problem. Six hours after an uneventful dental extraction the socket starts bleeding and keeps bleeding. APTT is mildly prolonged; factor VIII is 0.2 U/mL; factor IX and VWF are normal.
items.explanation: Two steps: **delayed** bleeding indicates a coagulation defect, and factor VIII of 0.2 U/mL falls in the **mild** range (> 0.05–0.4). This is mild haemophilia A, which often presents late.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman of Ashkenazi Jewish descent bleeds excessively after a tonsillectomy. APTT is prolonged and corrects on mixing. Factors VIII and IX and VWF are normal.
items.explanation: An isolated long APTT with normal VIII, IX and VWF leaves **factor XI**. Its deficiency (haemophilia C) is autosomal and commoner in Ashkenazi Jews, so women are affected too.

items.stem: A 4-year-old girl born to first-cousin parents has repeated severe nosebleeds needing transfusion. Bleeding time is prolonged, VWF is undetectable and factor VIII is markedly reduced.
items.explanation: Autosomal recessive inheritance (consanguinity), severe bleeding and **absent VWF** with secondarily very low VIII indicate **type 3 VWD**. Joint bleeds remain uncommon even in this type.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best match from the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: An 8-year-old boy with severe haemophilia A and a known high-titre factor VIII inhibitor has an acutely painful, swollen ankle today.
items.explanation: An inhibitor neutralises infused factor VIII, so an acute bleed needs a **bypassing agent**, here **recombinant VIIa** (FEIBA is the alternative).

items.stem: A 3-year-old boy with severe haemophilia A developed an inhibitor after his first few exposures to factor VIII. The long-term aim of his team is to eradicate the antibody so that standard factor VIII prophylaxis can resume.
items.explanation: **Immune tolerance induction** gets rid of the inhibitor in about 80% of patients, after which standard replacement works again.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man with mild haemophilia B (factor IX 0.1 U/mL) needs a dental extraction.
items.explanation: Haemophilia B needs **factor IX concentrate**. Desmopressin releases VIII and VWF only and does not work in B.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with untreated coeliac disease has bruising. PT and APTT are both prolonged; factor VIII and VWF are normal.
items.explanation: Malabsorption causes **vitamin K deficiency**, which lowers II, VII, IX and X and prolongs both PT and APTT. Treat with **phytomenadione**.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best match from the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A man with haemophilia A and his wife, who is not a carrier, ask about their newborn son. What is the chance that the son is affected?
items.explanation: A father passes his **Y chromosome** to sons, so an affected man cannot transmit haemophilia to his sons.

items.stem: A healthy woman whose father had haemophilia B is pregnant with a boy. What is the chance that he is affected?
items.explanation: Two steps: as the daughter of an affected man she is an **obligate carrier**, and each son of a carrier has a **50%** chance of being affected.

items.stem: The same woman asks, before her next pregnancy and without knowing the baby's sex, the chance of having an affected boy.
items.explanation: Each pregnancy of a carrier has a **1 in 4** chance of an affected boy (half are boys × half of those affected).

items.stem: A woman's brother has severe haemophilia A and her mother is a confirmed carrier. Her father is unaffected. What is the chance that she herself is a carrier?
items.explanation: Each daughter of a carrier mother has a **50%** chance of being a carrier. Because carrier factor VIII levels vary with lyonization, mutation analysis would settle it.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best match from the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Iliopsoas haematoma with femoral nerve compression

items.stem: A 32-year-old man with severe haemophilia A grew up without access to prophylaxis. Both knees have fixed flexion deformities with thigh muscle wasting. X-rays show loss of joint space, subchondral cysts, sclerosis and osteophytes.
items.explanation: Repeated haemarthroses cause synovial hypertrophy and cartilage destruction, which is **chronic haemophilic arthropathy**, the main long-term morbidity.

items.stem: A 12-year-old boy with severe haemophilia had an untreated, very tense and painful calf bleed last year. He now cannot get his heel to the floor because his Achilles tendon has shortened.
items.explanation: A calf haematoma in the tight fascial sheath causes **compartment syndrome**. The resulting ischaemia, necrosis and fibrosis contract and shorten the Achilles tendon.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy with haemophilia B has received factor IX for years without problems. During today's infusion he develops urticaria, wheeze and hypotension, and his next bleeds respond poorly to factor IX.
items.explanation: Inhibitors are rare in haemophilia B (< 1%), but when they occur they may first show as a **severe allergic-type reaction**.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man with mild haemophilia A is given desmopressin twice daily for three days after a minor operation. He becomes confused and drowsy; serum sodium is 121 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Repeated desmopressin causes **water retention and hyponatraemia**, so sodium must be monitored.

items.stem: A 25-year-old man with severe haemophilia A bangs his head on a kitchen cupboard. Two hours later he has a worsening headache and starts vomiting.
items.explanation: Intracranial bleeding is much commoner in haemophilia and is a leading cause of death. **Any head injury needs urgent assessment** and factor replacement.

questions.leadIn: Pick the best match from the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: VWF antigen and ristocetin cofactor activity

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman's brother has severe haemophilia A caused by an identified intron 22 inversion. Her factor VIII is 0.6 U/mL. She wants to know for certain whether she is a carrier.
items.explanation: Two steps: carrier factor VIII levels overlap with normal because of lyonization, so a normal level does not exclude carriage. **Mutation analysis** for the known family lesion is definitive.

items.stem: A 9-year-old with severe haemophilia A on prophylaxis now bleeds despite his usual doses. His APTT does not correct on mixing with normal plasma. The team wants to quantify the antibody.
items.explanation: Failure to correct on mixing indicates an inhibitor. The **Bethesda assay** measures its titre, which guides the choice between high-dose factor and bypassing agents.

items.stem: A boy with recurrent haemarthroses has an isolated prolonged APTT that corrects on mixing. His factor VIII level is normal.
items.explanation: A corrected APTT with normal VIII leaves the next intrinsic factor, so request a **factor IX assay** to look for haemophilia B.

items.stem: A boy is born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery to a mother who carries severe haemophilia A. He seems well.
items.explanation: Newborns with severe haemophilia are at increased risk of intracranial bleeding, so **cranial imaging within 24 hours** is advised.

items.stem: A 17-year-old girl has heavy periods and nosebleeds. Platelet count, PT and APTT are all normal.
items.explanation: VWD can present with a **normal APTT**, so mucocutaneous bleeding with a normal screen needs **VWF antigen and ristocetin cofactor testing**.

ospe.identify: Knee X-ray of **advanced haemophilic arthropathy**: no cartilage space between femur and tibia, sclerosis, osteophytes, bone cysts and **broadened femoral epicondyles**
Clinical photos: **chronic arthropathy** with joint swelling and muscle wasting, a **thigh muscle haematoma**, massive bruising and a **retroperitoneal bleed** in severe haemophilia
Queen Victoria's pedigree: **X-linked recessive** haemophilia B, with carrier females and affected males across generations
**Hepatoma in a cirrhotic liver** from HCV acquired through non-virally-inactivated factor concentrate
Lab grid: **haemophilia A** has a normal bleeding time and VWF with a long APTT; **VWD** has a long bleeding time and low VWF; **vitamin K deficiency** has a long PT
Factor VIII:C and VWF: defective VIII:C (X chromosome) with normal VWF in **haemophilia A** vs low VWF (chromosome 12), leaving VIII:C unprotected, in **VWD**
Flowchart for a **prolonged aPTT**: mixing study (corrects = deficiency, fails = inhibitor), then specific factor assays
